content: Cerealine, also referred to as malt flakes, was a widely consumed American cereal product in the 19th century and is recognized as the first dry breakfast food. Unlike corn flakes, which were introduced in 1898 and are made by rolling and toasting, Cerealine consisted of uncooked flakes made from corn grits. Initially, it was utilized in the brewing industry. Cerealine Flakes, commonly known simply as Cerealine, was also the brand name for a raw-flake cereal produced from grits by the Cerealine Manufacturing Company, based in Indianapolis, Indiana, USA. In the late 19th century, after its initial use in beer brewing, Cerealine became one of the three most popular cereals of the time, alongside cracked wheat and oatmeal. These cereals were typically sold by retailers in bulk, who would scoop them out of barrels and sell them by weight to customers. Eventually, Cerealine Flakes began to be sold in packaged form. White-corn Cerealine Flakes were invented, possibly by accident, by James Vannoy, a mill worker in Columbus, Indiana, around 1884 or 1887. The Cerealine Mill was constructed in 1867 by T.W. Gaff & Co., a distillery based in Aurora, Indiana, at 607 Jackson Street in Columbus, Indiana. The Cerealine Manufacturing Company later relocated to Indianapolis, Indiana, sometime before 1898. However, the original Columbus mill building remained intact and was restored in the late 20th or early 21st century. It was repurposed as a cafeteria and conference center by Cummins Inc., an engine manufacturing corporation. Before being annexed by Indianapolis in 1895, the area surrounding what was then known as the Cerealine Works was referred to as Cerealinetown.
